claims.claim: RFC-001 commits that impersonation 'can be enabled/disabled only at the system level. Once enabled/disabled, it is applicable to all Argo CD Applications', but the platform sync call decided the rollout goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide. The decided rollout model is one the design's Goals section explicitly rules out; one of the two must change.

T-26271's CI diff failure and RFC-001 describe the same change without saying so: the failing jobs began when 'the sync impersonation flag' was enabled, and RFC-001's impersonation swaps the sync identity from the control-plane service account to the AppProject's defaultServiceAccount. The reporter is chasing the broad cluster Secret credential, but the narrower identity is exactly what RFC-001's decoupling produces; the error shows server-side apply dry-run being denied RBAC grants the new identity does not hold.

Split-identity audit and review gap: with RFC-001 impersonation enabled, sync acts as the AppProject destinationServiceAccounts identity (which the Kubernetes audit trail captures per RFC-001's open question), but T-28695 shows the Server-Side Diff path still acts as the cluster Secret credential and forces repeated unbounded 'patch' grants onto that standing credential. Access review that follows the new impersonated identity will miss that the old shared credential is not only kept but progressively widened, round after round, to keep diffs working.

T-9095's open request (respect users' existing Kubernetes RBAC instead of duplicated Argo CD RBAC) and RFC-001's motivation (manage permissions 'using kubernetes native RBAC implementation rather than using complex configurations in AppProjects') converge on the same access model from two directions: RFC-001 delivers it for the sync identity only, while T-9095 asks for it for UI-initiated user actions (pod delete, exec). If RFC-001 ships without acknowledging T-9095, the org runs two RBAC regimes: cluster-native for machine syncs, Argo-CD-internal for the human actions T-9095 covers, and reviewers must audit both.

T-27833's proposal is a per-resource split (namespace bootstrap via the Argo CD SA, everything else via the impersonated SA), but RFC-001 already decided 'The service account to be used for impersonation is determined on a per Application level rather than on per resource level.' The requested control cannot be built on the shipped design without reopening that decision; neither document names the other.

The strategy's roadmap states 'Deletion of generated Applications is explicitly out of scope for rollout orchestration: ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented. Teardown remains a manual operator action, performed one Application at a time.' The PRD proposes exactly that: a deletionOrder field (AllAtOnce/Reverse) implementing ordered, automated deletion of ApplicationSet children. Both commitments cannot hold; note-2 flags the disagreement but assigns no owner.

The PRD's Risks and Mitigations section says 'No immediate Risks to consider', but T-28511 is field evidence of a live failure of the same mechanism: a rollingSync step order with the reverse deletion strategy, whose wait-for-full-deletion never completes on a stuck Progressing resource, producing an infinite delete/re-create loop reproduced in staging per the incident review. The PRD's risk claim and the filed incident cannot both stand.

The strategy prescribes teardown as 'a manual operator action, performed one Application at a time' — and manual out-of-band deletion of a Progressive Sync child is precisely the trigger for T-28511's delete/recreate loop (Application 'deleted manually outside of its purview (e.g. in ArgoCD UI)'). The strategy's own recommended operating procedure walks operators into the known incident until the controller fix lands.

PRD Reverse deletion is defined as 'the reverse order of the steps configured in RollingSync strategy', while T-28755 proposes parallel rollingSync steps (parallel/parallelGroups) where steps are no longer a single sequence. If both ship, 'reverse order of the steps' is ill-defined for parallel groups; neither document accounts for the other, and the PRD's check that 'rollingSync lists out an order' would reject or misorder parallel configurations.

T-27949's pilot symptom and RFC-002's design are the same underlying change: RFC-002's hydrator pushes a fresh commit to the syncSource targetBranch on every hydration cycle, and T-27949 reports that on a hydrator-pilot repository 'every hydration cycle lands a fresh commit on the hydrated branch... and each of those commits is picked up as a source change', restarting the RollingSync wave. RFC-002 does not acknowledge any interaction with Progressive Sync; the incident review confirmed the wave-restart mechanism.

The incident review's interim restriction — 'hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until there's a debounce' — blocks more than the pilot ticket it was written against: T-24578 plans Source Hydrator support for ApplicationSets, whose entire mechanism is hydrated Applications driven by ApplicationSet ordering, and the strategy's ApplicationSet first-class support direction inherits the same collision. Neither plan records the restriction, so both are scheduled as if it were lifted.

RFC-002's push-to-stage mode 'relies on some external system to move changes to the deployment branch', T-26443 documents the failure mode when that mover lags ('the external promoter has not yet moved the fresh manifests to the deployment branch, so auto-sync picks up whatever the stage branch last held' — syncing stale manifests), and note-1 records that the promoter is still an unowned shell script ('our stage-branch promoter is still the shell script, nobody owns it'). The integration point the design depends on is both failure-prone in the field and ownerless.

RFC-002's Goal 4 is 'Every deployed change must have a corresponding dry commit - i.e. git is always the source of any changes', and push-to-stage exists as the integration point for promotion systems. T-27327 proposes that rollback 'directly updates the sync branch (bypassing the staging branch)' by checking out old rendered manifests with no new dry commit — a deployed change whose lineage the dry branch does not carry and which skips the promotion path the RFC reserves. The two commitments cannot both hold as written.

T-24417's motivation and RFC-002's 'Handling External Values Files' decision are opposite sides of the same design choice: RFC-002 resolves the single-dry-source limitation by recommending 'users use the umbrella chart approach' (Helm dependencies), while T-24417 reports that 'switching to helm dependencies... makes it difficult to use with ApplicationSets to control the chart version across environments' and asks for Chart support in DrySource instead. The ticket is field pushback against the RFC's stated recommendation without citing it.

Machine-authored writes enter the system of record without provable machine authorship: RFC-002's commit server pushes hydrated commits using a repository-write GitHub App credential while templating the dry commit's human commitAuthor into the README/metadata, and T-28239 confirms the hydrator 'always pushes unsigned commits' — signing is only proposed, opt-in, default false. Until commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits ships and is enabled, nothing distinguishes a legitimate hydrator push from any other holder of the repository-write secret; an organization adopting RFC-002's Use case 1 (strong change auditing) cannot prove provenance of the deployed branch. Whether this breaches any specific audit commitment is a question for counsel, not settled here.

T-28927 plans to promote Progressive Sync to Stable ('tested and validated with various use cases'), but T-27846 records that the observability needed to validate it is still an open request ('getting a wide-eye view of progressive sync is difficult' — no metrics for wave timing, refresh counts, or why a sync is not starting), and T-27949 notes controller logs at warn level emitted no progressive-sync transition logs during a live failure. The stable promotion depends on measurement that does not exist yet, and the dependency is stated nowhere.

The debounce restriction from the incident review has no way to be verified as fixed: confirming that hydrator pushes stop restarting rolling sync waves requires exactly the metric T-27846 requests ('How much Application refresh were caused by the ApplicationSet'), which is unbuilt. The interim restriction on hydrator pilot repos therefore has no measurable exit criterion; nobody can show the number that would justify lifting it.

T-28695 and T-26271 are the same underlying design gap surfacing in two components — the diff path not honoring the impersonation identity that RFC-001 gives the sync path. T-28695 itself scopes T-26271 as 'same error string, different component' (argocd-server CLI diff in-cluster vs application-controller reconcile on external clusters); note-1's root-cause ('diff runs as the destination service account which doesn't hold patch on cluster-scoped stuff') and T-28695's finding (diff runs as the cluster credential) describe different components' identities, which is precisely why the tickets keep being scoped past each other.

T-26443's stale-sync symptom and T-27875's skipped-auto-sync root cause meet at the same mechanism: auto-sync acting on a revision the app never actually deployed. T-27875 shows Status.Sync.Revision reflects the last compared, not last synced, revision; T-26443 shows auto-sync eagerly deploying whatever the sync-source branch last held. Any fix to hydrator sync-freshness (T-26443's annotation proposal) that keys off compared-revision state inherits T-27875's compared-vs-synced confusion.

proposals.change: Record the root cause from the platform sync call: with impersonation enabled, the diff runs as the destination service account, which lacks patch on cluster-scoped resources — the broad cluster Secret credential is not the acting identity, so the reporter should stop investigating it.
proposals.citedLine: the CI diff failures (the missing-permissions one, T-26271) got root-caused on the call: with impersonation on, diff runs as the destination service account which doesn't hold patch on cluster-scoped stuff. someone should note the root cause on that ticket so the reporter stops chasing the cluster secret.

proposals.change: Record that this work is deprioritized to next quarter and the dev pair has moved to the progressive sync deletion loop.
proposals.citedLine: hydrator rollback work (the history & rollback ticket, T-27327) is deprioritized to next quarter. dev pair moves to the progressive sync deletion loop instead. ticket should say so.

proposals.change: Record the staging reproduction (reverse deletion order) and the incident-runbook mitigation: switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before manually deleting any child Application, until the controller fix lands.
proposals.citedLine: the delete/recreate loop (T-28511) reproduced in staging with the reverse deletion order. mitigation for now: incident runbook says switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand. that's the operational rule until the controller fix lands — worth remembering as a standing practice.

proposals.change: Record the interim restriction from the incident review: hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists, and note the confirmed mechanism that each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave.
proposals.citedLine: interim call from the review: hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until there's a debounce. the pilot ticket (T-27949) should carry that restriction so the next team doesn't trip it.

deltas.body: Decision: the impersonation rollout goes behind a per-project flag rather than fleet-wide, and no project enables it until the diff-identity story is fixed. This contradicts RFC-001's stated goal of system-level-only enablement and needs to be reflected there.
deltas.citedLine: impersonation rollout: we decided it goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide. nobody flips it on a project until the diff story is fixed. that's a real decision, not a maybe.

deltas.body: Standing operational rule (incident runbook): before manually deleting any child Application of a Progressive Sync ApplicationSet, switch the ApplicationSet's deletion to AllAtOnce; this holds until the controller fix for the delete/recreate loop lands.
deltas.citedLine: mitigation for now: incident runbook says switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand. that's the operational rule until the controller fix lands — worth remembering as a standing practice.

deltas.body: Standing interim restriction: repositories piloting the source hydrator must not use progressive sync until a debounce for hydrator-push-triggered wave restarts exists. This constrains all hydrator+ApplicationSet plans, not just the pilot.
deltas.citedLine: interim call from the review: hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until there's a debounce.

deltas.body: Open fact not in any record: the stage-branch promoter that push-to-stage mode depends on is still a shell script with no owner. It was parked, not resolved, and needs an owner given T-26443's stale-sync failure mode runs through it.
deltas.citedLine: also priya flagged that our stage-branch promoter is still the shell script, nobody owns it. parking that.

deltas.body: Unowned open question: the strategy document still says ApplicationSet deletion stays a manual operator action while the PRD proposes ordered automated deletion; the review acknowledged the disagreement but explicitly did not decide it, and it needs an owner.
deltas.citedLine: someone asked whether the strategy doc still says appset deletion stays manual — if the PRD ships ordered deletion those two disagree, needs an owner. not deciding here.
